headline: Big Tech's AI Infrastructure Spree: Over $1 Trillion Spent, $745 Billion More Expected in 2026
summary: Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft have collectively invested over $1.1 trillion in AI infrastructure since 2023, with projections indicating an additional $745 billion will be spent this year alone.
details: Four major tech companies – Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft – have poured more than $1.1 trillion into AI infrastructure, encompassing data centers, chips, and power, since 2023. Financial Times reports that an additional $745 billion is anticipated for this year, highlighting the immense scale of investment.

This surge in capital expenditure is impacting various sectors. Increased power demand from data centers is forcing utility companies to upgrade infrastructure, with costs passed on to consumers. Environmental concerns are also leading to community pushback against new data center projects.

The demand for AI hardware, particularly High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), is significantly affecting the chip industry. Tech giants are willing to pay premium prices, leading manufacturers like Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix to prioritize HBM over traditional DRAM. This has resulted in shortages of consumer memory impacting PCs, smartphones, and even the automotive industry.

Experts are raising concerns about the financial implications of these massive AI investments. Some warn of 'hidden debt' amounting to approximately $1.65 trillion, annotated as future obligations in financial statements, potentially misrepresenting the companies' true liabilities to investors.

Despite the colossal spending, these companies continue to generate substantial revenue. Microsoft reported $90 billion, Meta $60 billion, Alphabet nearly $120 billion, and Amazon $200 billion in their latest quarterly earnings, totaling nearly $470 billion in a single quarter.

However, the financial strain is becoming apparent. Google's cloud business experienced its first quarterly loss since its IPO, and Meta's stock price dipped following announcements of plans to rent out its AI compute capacity, mirroring strategies by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.
